performers: Alisa Weilerstein, cello; Jason Yoder, marimba
intro: Alisa Weilerstein plays The Swan, the thirteenth movement of Le Carnaval des animaux, at the White House with Jason Yoder, a sixteen-year-old marimba player. He plays the accompaniment on the marimba beneath her bowed melody.

sections.label: B · Melody climbs and turns, cello and marimba
sections.mNote: The cello holds long notes over separate marimba strokes

sections.label: C · Cello melody over marimba
sections.mNote: The marimba plays continuous broken chords under the cello.

cues.title: Cello and marimba, White House, 2009
cues.text: Saint-Saëns wrote a long cello melody over continuous broken chords. In this arrangement the chords go to a marimba. On 4 November 2009 at the White House, Jason Yoder played them with mallets on the instrument’s wooden bars, and Alisa Weilerstein played the cello line.
cues.evidence: The official White House video shows Yoder playing marimba beside Weilerstein on 4 November 2009: https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/photos-and-video/video/alisa-weilerstein-and-jason-yoder-perform-white-house-5-8. The original cello melody and accompaniment are in Durand score D.S. 3891.

cues.title: White House performance, 2009
cues.text: Jason Yoder was sixteen when he joined the cellist Alisa Weilerstein for the White House’s Evening of Classical Music on 4 November 2009. The cello solo was played as a duet for cello and percussion.
cues.evidence: The official White House description names cellist Alisa Weilerstein and sixteen-year-old percussionist Jason Yoder, and dates the event to 4 November 2009: https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/photos-and-video/video/alisa-weilerstein-and-jason-yoder-perform-white-house-5-8

cues.title: Final bars, cello
cues.text: In the closing bars the cello melody slows and ends on a high G. The accompaniment continues under the held note and goes on after it stops. Saint-Saëns leaves the soloist silent at the end while the last broken chords complete the phrase.
cues.evidence: Durand score, plate D.S. 3891, p. 3, final five bars; Carl Fischer cello part (1907), final line. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/5/5f/IMSLP925269-PMLP06099-2024-03-15-12-42-19-01.PDF
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Pianist from the age of ten and organist for twenty years, known for the Organ Symphony, a dance of skeletons featuring xylophone, and a zoo suite he forbade anyone to publish.
facts: Piano with Stamaty; organ with François Benoist and composition under Halévy at the Paris Conservatoire, from 1848
Organist of La Madeleine, 1857–77; piano professor at the École Niedermeyer, 1861–65; co-founder of the Société nationale de musique, 1871
Symphonies, ten concertos, four symphonic poems, operas, organ music, songs and chamber music; also plays, poems and articles
Spent most winters from 1873 in Algeria, Egypt or the Canary Islands, and kept no fixed address from 1889 to 1905

quote.text: I have given it all that I had to give. What I have done I shall never do again.
quote.source: Saint-Saëns on the Organ Symphony, as quoted in Hugh Macdonald’s Boston Symphony Orchestra note

composer.background:
Camille Saint-Saëns was born at 3 rue du Jardinet in Paris on 9 October 1835. His father, a clerk in the Ministry of the Interior, died of consumption on 30 December, when the boy was not yet three months old. He was a sickly child and was raised by two widows, his mother Clémence and her aunt Charlotte Masson, who taught him piano. At two and a half he pressed the keys one at a time and waited for each note to die away before playing the next. By his own account he already listened at that age to the kettle on the drawing-room fire, which he called a “microscopic oboe”, and to its sound swelling until the water boiled.

Children’s pieces gave the left hand nothing to do. “The bass doesn’t sing,” he told his teachers in disgust, and was given Haydn and Mozart. On 6 May 1846, aged ten, he played Beethoven’s Third Piano Concerto and a Mozart concerto in B♭ at the Salle Pleyel, and played the whole programme from memory. Someone asked his mother what he would play when he was twenty. “He will play his own,” she said.
